newsitem.title: Cyprus: Britain says arms build-up on Cyprus is dangerous.
newsitem.headline: Britain says arms build-up on Cyprus is dangerous.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Monday that further militarisation of divided Cyprus would be a mistake which might scupper efforts to start peace talks early next year.

Both the internationally recognised government in the Greek Cypriot part of the Mediterranean island and the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north have been beefing up defences and Rifkind said the levels of armaments were "dangerously high".
"You cannot have a degree of military presence without the risk that it might be used," he told reporters after meeting Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides on Monday morning.

Rifkind argued against further militarisation, saying: "That would be something which would be a big step in the wrong direction and that is a point which I believe should be understood by all concerned."
The Turkish-occupied north has about 35,000 troops, while Greek Cypriot forces number about 11,500.
Rifkind, first British foreign secretary to visit Cyprus for more than 30 years, argues that the world wants to see an end to a conflict that it regards as a throwback to an earlier age.
Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 and occupied the northern third of the island in response to a short-lived coup engineered by the military junta ruling in Greece at the time.
Turkey, Greece and Britain, the former colonial power until independence in 1960, are guarantor powers of Cyprus.

International mediators are boosting efforts to bring the two sides together in peace talks in early 1997. Rifkind said he was encouraged at the extent to which Clerides wanted to see real progress next year.

Later in the day Rifkind is due to cross the United Nations patrolled "Green Line" which divides the capital and meet with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, leader of a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state declared in 1983 and recognised only by Ankara.
"A similar approach (to Clerides) could be very encouraging but I cannot anticipate that. I must wait to see Mr Denktash and I will come to my own judgment as to what the opportunities are."
Rifkind, aware that the United Nations has nothing to show for decades of attempts to broker peace, was at pains to stress that any progress would be slow.

"I think there is a real scope for progress but one must acknowledge that is not going to happen overnight but that 1997 ought to be the year in which perhaps the important breakthrough is made," he said.
Rifkind got an insight into the passions dividing the two communities when a small group of elderly Greek Cypriot women on Sunday begged him to help find relatives missing since the Turkish invasion.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said last week that the situation on Cyprus this year was the worst since the 1974 invasion. Four people have been killed in ceasefire line incidents since August.
British officials said one pressure point that Rifkind might use would be the talks that Cyprus is due to start on becoming a member of the European Union.
"We want to use the accession talks to give momentum to a political process which has been quiet for too long," one said.
The Cyprus membership talks, set to start six months after the EU completes its inter-governmental conference on reforming the 15-nation bloc, could begin in 1998.
